decision.question: To kick things off, walk me through how you connected your React and Vite frontend to your FastAPI backend on day 3.
decision.rationale: The candidate gave a minimal greeting. Need to prompt them to start discussing the Day 3 objectives regarding the React/FastAPI setup.

turns.answer: We just used fetch from React to hit the FastAPI endpoints. Had to add CORS middleware because it kept erroring at first.

objectivesHit: Connect the React frontend with the FastAPI backend

Had to add CORS middleware because it kept erroring at first

decision.question: Which specific FastAPI endpoint were you hitting with fetch, and how did you configure the CORS middleware?
decision.rationale: The candidate mentioned using fetch and adding CORS, but left out specifics on the route or configuration. Asking for the endpoint and CORS setup tests specificity.

turns.answer: It was /api/chat I think. For CORS I just copied the middleware setup from the docs and used allow_origins with a wildcard.

objectivesHit: Connect the React frontend with the FastAPI backend

decision.question: Before wiring up the frontend, how did you test your prompt loop directly against the local Ollama model in the CLI?
decision.rationale: Candidate answered on endpoints and CORS. Moving to probe the command-line chatbot and Ollama aspect of Day 3.

turns.answer: I just ran the python script in the terminal and typed questions to see what came back. Ollama was running locally so it was pretty quick.

objectivesHit: Build a command-line chatbot powered by your local Ollama model

claims.text: ran the python script in the terminal and typed questions

decision.question: When you set up the FastAPI backend, how did you structure the health endpoint to check if the service was up?
decision.rationale: Candidate gave a general description of running the CLI script. Specificity is low, and we need to cover the remaining Day 3 objectives like the FastAPI health endpoint.

turns.answer: Standard /health returning a 200 with a JSON status. But the useful thing was making it check the Ollama connection too, not just that FastAPI was alive — a liveness check that only proves the web server is up will happily report healthy while the model backend is down, so the container never gets restarted.

objectivesHit: Scaffold a FastAPI backend with a health endpoint

claims.text: Standard /health returning a 200 with a JSON status
making it check the Ollama connection too
liveness check that only proves the web server is up will happily report healthy while the model backend is down

decision.question: How did you actually code that Ollama check inside the health endpoint?
decision.rationale: The candidate correctly distinguished liveness from dependency health checks. Pushing deeper to see the implementation detail of how they queried Ollama within the health route.

turns.answer: Just a try/except around a request to the Ollama endpoint. If it came back, healthy, if not, 503.

claims.text: Just a try/except around a request to the Ollama endpoint
If it came back, healthy, if not, 503

turns.answer: I don't think we really had a router. It just always did the vector search and if nothing came back we'd say we couldn't find it.

claims.text: I don't think we really had a router

decision.question: Moving to Day 22 — how did your router agent decide which healthcare specialist agent to send a request to?
decision.rationale: The candidate lacked a router on Day 10. Transitioning to Day 22 to examine how they implemented the router agent for multi-agent orchestration.

turns.answer: That was mostly LangChain's agent stuff. We gave it the tools and it picked. I couldn't really tell you how it decided.

decision.rationale: The candidate did not provide an answer regarding Day 28 containerization, so we are moving directly to the Day 31 capstone project to examine the integrated system.

feedback.summary: You walked through key architectural details of your enterprise healthcare chatbot, showing particular clarity around API integration and backend health monitoring. Your explanation of dependency health checks was a highlight of the conversation. When the discussion moved toward query routing mechanisms, agent orchestration under the hood, and Docker base configuration, your explanations thinned out.
strengths: You articulated a clear architectural reason for probing model dependencies in your health endpoint, noting that "a liveness check that only proves the web server is up will happily report healthy while the model backend is down, so the container never gets restarted."
You described the practical HTTP error handling logic for that check plainly: "Just a try/except around a request to the Ollama endpoint. If it came back, healthy, if not, 503."

You clearly described how you wired up the initial communication between your frontend and API: "We just used fetch from React to hit the FastAPI endpoints. Had to add CORS middleware because it kept erroring at first."
gaps: When asked about query routing between SQL and vector engines, you explained that the system relied solely on a basic fallback path: "I don't think we really had a router. It just always did the vector search and if nothing came back we'd say we couldn't find it."

When explaining how multi-agent choices were made, the underlying selection logic wasn't fully unpacked: "That was mostly LangChain's agent stuff. We gave it the tools and it picked. I couldn't really tell you how it decided."
The question regarding your Dockerfile base image configuration was left unanswered: "Answer:"
next: Open your Day 22 agent code and inspect the tool descriptions and system prompts you passed into LangChain to see exactly how the model selects which tool to execute.
Check your Day 28 Dockerfile in your repository to confirm the exact base image name and tag you built your backend container on.
Look at your Day 10 retrieval code and draft a simple conditional check or classification step before the vector lookup to see how you would route incoming requests based on content.
